html:
The Confederated Tribes of Grand Ronde are a union of more than 27 Native peoples of western Oregon, grouped together on the Grand Ronde Reservation in 1856. The map shows their homelands in 1492, from the Oregon coast to the Cascades and from the Columbia River to northern California.

Among them were the Kalapuya of the Willamette Valley, the Molalla, the Umpqua, the Shasta and Rogue River peoples, and bands of the Chinook. After the Rogue River Wars of 1855 and 1856, the army marched survivors north to the new reservation.

Because the bands had long traded with one another, many people already spoke the trade language of the region. On the reservation it became an everyday creole, Chinook Wawa, which the tribe now teaches to children.

The United States ended its recognition of the tribe in 1954 and restored it in 1983. Its neighbour to the west is the Siletz confederation, formed the same way.
